lesson.title: Raising a Limit to a Power: The Power Rule
lesson.summary: The power rule says that if f(x) approaches L as x approaches a, then f(x) raised to a whole number power n approaches L raised to that same power, since repeated multiplication of a limit by itself just repeats the product rule.
lesson.body:
Once the product rule is available, raising a function to a whole number power is not really a new idea, just the same idea applied several times in a row. If f(x) is closing in on L, then f(x) times f(x) closes in on L times L, by the product rule with both factors equal to f. Multiplying by another copy of f(x) closes that new product in on another factor of L, and so on. Repeating this process n minus 1 times, once for each additional factor of f(x) beyond the first, shows why raising a limit to a power behaves exactly the way you would hope.

The Power Rule for Limits states that if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L, and n is a positive whole number, then the limit of f(x) raised to the n as x approaches a equals L raised to the n. The rule extends further, with a bit more care, to roots and fractional powers: the limit of the square root of f(x) as x approaches a equals the square root of L, provided L is greater than or equal to 0, so that the square root is a real number to begin with. Similar statements hold for other roots, with the parallel requirement that the relevant root of L makes sense as a real number.

Here is a worked example using a whole number power. Let f(x) equal x minus 1, and find the limit of f(x) cubed as x approaches 3. First, the limit of x minus 1 as x approaches 3 is 2. By the power rule, the limit of (x minus 1) cubed as x approaches 3 is 2 cubed, which equals 8. Checking directly, (x minus 1) cubed at x equals 3 is 2 cubed, again 8. The two computations agree.

Here is a second worked example using a root. Find the limit of the square root of x plus 5, as x approaches 4. The limit of x plus 5 as x approaches 4 is 9, and since 9 is greater than or equal to 0, the square root version of the power rule applies: the limit of the square root of x plus 5 equals the square root of 9, which is 3. Checking directly, the square root of (4 plus 5) is the square root of 9, again 3. Both methods agree, and this second example shows exactly the kind of expression that reappears when rationalizing techniques are needed for limits involving square roots.

The power rule matters beyond its own computations because it is the last piece needed to justify a much bigger shortcut. Once sums, products, constant multiples, and powers of limits are all known to behave the way plain substitution would suggest, any expression built from x and constants using those operations, meaning any polynomial, inherits that same behavior automatically. That observation is exactly what makes direct substitution work, which is the next idea to explore.

It is worth being precise about why the power rule needs n to be a positive whole number in its basic form. The argument that builds it out of the product rule only makes sense when there is a specific finite number of copies of f(x) being multiplied together, since the product rule itself only combines a fixed, countable number of functions at a time. Extending the idea to negative whole number powers, meaning reciprocals, or to powers that are fractions, meaning roots, requires bringing in the quotient rule or the extra conditions on the sign of L mentioned above, rather than following automatically from the product rule alone. Keeping that distinction in mind helps explain why the root version of the power rule needed the extra condition that L be nonnegative, while the whole number power version needed no such condition at all.
